introduction:
The function of ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) is dependent on protein–
protein and protein–RNA interactions. Chemical crosslinking with
mass spectrometry [XL-MS (Leitner et al., 2016); Fig. 1, top right] is
used for mapping protein–protein interactions. On the other hand,
the detection of RNA-linked peptides by mass spectrometry (MS) is
challenging, given complex MS signals of low intensity (Schmidt
et al., 2012). This challenge is met by the RBDmap method: allow-
ing to detect protein–RNA interactions using UV crosslinking fol-
lowed by tandem proteolysis, using LysC or ArgC followed by
trypsin, combined with MS (Castello et al., 2016, 2017; Zhang
et al., 2019) (Fig. 1, top left). Software packages are available for
initial processing of XL-MS data [e.g. pLink (Yang et al., 2012)] or
RBDmap data [e.g. MaxQuant (Tyanova et al., 2016)]. However, in
an RBDmap experiment, the MS-identified peptides are adjacent to
the RNA-linked peptides (Castello et al., 2016, 2017). Therefore,
downstream bioinformatic analysis reveals the RNA-linked pepti-
des, given the protein sequence and the proteases used in the assay.
Hence, custom pipelines are needed to combine, compare or reduce
datasets obtained from different experiments, treatments and repli-
cates, especially if RBDmap is complemented by XL-MS. Such cus-
tom analysis has remained a bottleneck for the study of RNP
complexes when both protein–protein and protein–RNA interac-
tions are of interest.
Herein, we describe crisscrosslinkeR, an R package aimed to
identify molecular interactions detected from both types of XL-MS
experiments—XL-MS and RBDmap—and to map both protein–

and Degiacomi et al. 2017)]. crisscrosslinkeR was designed to fill
the gap between the primary analysis of MS data to the interpret-
ation and visualization of the results either simultaneously for both
protein–RNA interactions and protein–protein interactions, or in-
dependently for any of them. To our knowledge, it is the first tool
that streamlines RBDmap data analysis and the first package dedi-
cated for mapping both RBDmap and XL-MS data.
2 Implementation
Primary MS data analysis is performed by pLink (Yang et al., 2012),
MaxQuant (Tyanova et al., 2016) and Andromeda (Cox et al.,
2011), which identify tryptic peptides from raw MS files (.raw)
(Fig. 1, middle). In the context of the MS data analysis pipeline,
crisscrosslinkeR is placed downstream of these software and utilizes
R packages and APIs for protein data bank (PDB) file reading and
the RCSB PDB mapping.
3 Features
Data reduction is done across multiple samples, allowing to merge
replicates or accept data points based on user-defined conditions
(e.g. only if the same crosslinked peptide appeared in n replicates).
Filtration is based on significance scores that were assigned during
the primary data analysis. crisscrosslinkeR is designed to handle an
unlimited number of XL-MS and RBDmap datasets simultaneously
for a direct comparison or data reduction, based on user preference.
There are currently no tools to visualize RBDmap data over
sequences [two-dimensional (2D) visualization] or structures (3D
visualization) of protein complexes, though these forms of visualiza-
tion are popular and supported in case of XL-MS. crisscrosslinkeR
illustrate replicates or different experimental treatments for 2D rep-
resentation of RBDmap data. For 2D visualization of XL-MS and,
optionally, RBDmap data, crisscrosslinkeR exports files compatible
with the user-friendly server xiView (Graham et al., 2019) (Fig. 1,
bottom right). For 3D visualization of RBDmap and XL-MS data,
crisscrosslinkeR uses the RCSB PDB mapping API to identify the
most suitable 3D structure(s) in the PDB, aligns it to the sequence of
the protein used during the experiment and then uses the selected
structure for 3D visualization of either RBDmap or XL-MS data
(Fig. 1, bottom left). Specifically, crisscrosslinkeR generates a
Python script to launch PyMOL (Schrodinger, 2015)—a popular
and stable suite for molecular imaging—to generate publication-
quality figures or for structural analysis. crisscrosslinkeR can be
used to hide or present color-coded crosslinking sites, including
based on the score applied by the primary software that detected
them [MaxQuant (Tyanova et al., 2016) or pLink (Yang et al.,
2012)], the number of times linked peptides was detected across
multiple replicates and differential crosslinked sites and, when ap-
plicable, the Euclidean crosslinking distances; all these are visualized
with large flexibility for user-defined color selection.
Collectively, crisscrosslinkeR is a versatile pipeline that stream-
lines the workflow, starting from multiple raw data files down to
publication-quality figures.
discussion:
crisscrosslinkeR provides users with the ability to analyze and visual-
ize data obtained from both RBDmap and XL-MS experiments
including
an
unlimited
number
of
replicates
and
treatments.
crisscrosslinkeR allows the user to combine replicates, or to search
for common crosslinking events among replicates or different treat-
ments, in order to discover biological cues in a complex dataset.
These functionalities are complemented by 2D and 3D visualization,
tailored for subsequent communication of the results. The current
version of crisscrosslinker does not support solvent-accessible distan-
ces. These can be obtained using other software packages as Xwalk
(Kahraman et al. 2011) Jwalk (Bullock et al. 2018) and DynamXL
(Degiacomi et al. 2017). To our knowledge, crisscrosslinkeR is the
first available package that streamlines XL-MS data analysis for the
discovery of both protein–protein and protein–RNA interactions
within the same macromolecular RNP complex or biological system.
